"The Story" is sung by **Brandi Carlile**, but it was actually written by her bandmate **Phil Hanseroth**.

Phil Hanseroth composed the song before he even started playing with Brandi Carlile in a band. The song became one of Carlile's signature songs and was featured prominently on her 2007 album of the same name. It gained additional popularity after being covered by actress Sara Ramirez on *Grey's Anatomy* in 2007, and later by LeAnn Rimes and Dolly Parton.

Interestingly, while Phil Hanseroth wrote the song, he has consistently shared songwriting credits with all members of their group, as is their collaborative tradition.

Actually, no.
Her bandmate Phil Hanseroth wrote “The Story” before they even started playing together.
Since her debut, all of the music appearing under the name Brandi Carlile has been the product of an extraordinarily close partnership of Carlile and the twin brothers Tim and Phil Hanseroth. All three write songs and share the writing credits equally for every song regardless of who contributes what (à la Lennon and McCartney).
The three musicians connected in Seattle, where the twins played in the hard-rock band the Fighting Machinists while Carlile, raised on Patsy Cline and the Grand Ole Opry, was busking and doing bar gigs.
After the Fighting Machinists disbanded, Carlile recruited the twins to play with her; they first performed together in 2000, got matching tattoos (of the auryn talisman from _The NeverEnding Story,_ a movie they all loved as kids), and started collaborating on songs rooted in country, rock, and folk.
In this excerpt from a 2014 interview with me for _Acoustic Guitar_ magazine _,_ Carlile and the twins spoke with me about “The Story” and their style of collaboration.
The full interview is available is the May 2015 issue of _Acoustic Guitar_ or on Patreon.

### The story behind "The Story"
_It’s so hard to imagine that “The Story” existed before you started playing together. How did the original version compare with Brandi’s version?_
PHIL It doesn’t even compare at all. We had recorded a couple versions, like one on a keyboard and one with acoustic guitars. It was just a lyric, a melody, a couple of chords—it wasn’t really anything until we started playing with Brandi and she was able to put some power into it.
BRANDI “The Story” was already a beautiful song. Phil’s got a really powerful voice and sounded great singing it. But I think the song needed to be really loved by someone. If anything, I brought to the scenario a little bit of insanity and intensity and cultishness. Especially when I was younger, I was a little overwhelming. I came on the scene and I was like, “All right, let’s quit our jobs and get matching tattoos and never look back! I don’t care—forget about your wives, forget about everything, let’s just do this!”
TIM When we first met Brandi, she was playing primarily acoustic guitar, and my brother and I were still playing only electric guitar in a hard rock band. It was such an odd thing. We met Brandi and got into the acoustic guitar with her, and then six months later we were both getting divorces and had a bunch of tattoos, I swear! It was a big shift for everyone musically, and also we found our Charles Manson [_laughter_]. My brother and I have always had a close musical thing, but we finally found our third sibling.
_How would you characterize each other’s strengths as songwriters?_
BRANDI Well, I’ve got a pretty good grip on that. Phil writes these interesting and androgynous powerhouse songs, very infrequently. They’re usually kind of strange lyrically. I don’t think he really forces it. “Blood Muscle Skin & Bone,” “The Story,” “Oh Dear,” “Beginning to Feel the Years”—those are some of our more quirky _Pet Sounds_ type tunes, and they come from the terrifying mind of Phil.

### The story behind "The Story"
And then Tim, in my opinion, is your classic, workman-style songwriter who writes so many more songs than Phil and I do, and he writes them with such strength and continuity. I think they are our flagship songs on every record. When you hear a song that was started or penned by Tim, it sounds like the Brandi Carlile trio.
With me, it’s a real crap shoot, because it has to do so much with what’s going on in my life, and it’s based solely on lyrics. I tend to focus on my feelings and my environment lyrically. I like to really say what I mean and mean what I say, and say things that are special. So all three of us bring something interesting to the band. Tim brings total consistency and a prolific nature, Phil brings eccentricity, and I bring communication.
_Why did you decide to share songwriting credits for all of your songs?_
BRANDI Because there’s no ego. The music wins and takes precedence. Nobody questions anybody else if they really think that a bridge would make a song better or a lyric should change or we could add more interesting chords.
TIM It’s been like that since the very beginning. When we first met, it was like, hey, if we’re going to write songs together, let’s just split everything up. That way you’re not stuck being in a band with someone who’s doing really really well—
BRANDI Driving a red car.
TIM We all end up having to tour the same amount together, we spend an incredible amount of time together, and even though one of us may write a song that’s a hit for ten years, like Phil did here, we’re all putting about the same amount of work into it.
We don’t get too precious about our songwriting. If one of us has an idea that’s half done, nobody’s going to get possessive because they want the credit for it. Nobody’s going to get their feelings hurt by going, yeah, I want to write this one alone. We are all really open to just the song being the best.
_On the albums, though, you do credit who individually wrote each song. Why?_

### The story behind "The Story"
BRANDI For me, just because my heroes do. When I read the liner notes, I want to know. I’m really big into entertainers, and when I love an artist, I love everything about them. I love their philanthropy, I love their biography, their childhood stories, their artwork, the liner notes, and the songwriting. If I hear a song that I think is deeply personal, I want to know who wrote it and if it’s about what I think it’s about.

"**The Story**" is a song released as a single by American folk rock singer Brandi Carlile, written by Phil Hanseroth, from her 2007 album _The Story_. It’s one of Carlile's best-known songs and has been included in the setlist of all of her concert tours to date.
The song was featured in _[Grey's Anatomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's\_Anatomy "Grey's Anatomy")_ on April 12, 2007 and is on [Grey's Anatomy Soundtrack album 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Anatomy_(soundtrack) "Grey's Anatomy (soundtrack)") (released September 11, 2007). It received renewed attention when a cover version was recorded by _Grey's Anatomy_ actor Sara Ramirez and included in the 2011 musical episode "Song Beneath the Song". The track was later covered by LeAnn Rimes for her _Remnants_ album, and by Dolly Parton for the charity tribute album _Cover Stories_.

## Composition and recording
[edit]
Twin brothers Phil and Tim Hanseroth have been Carlile's performing and writing partners since 2004[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Faber-1) and "The Story" was written by Phil Hanseroth before the Hanseroths began collaborating with Carlile.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Chinen-2) It has a 16-bar melody.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Chinen-2) It was recorded in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada and produced by T-Bone Burnett.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-3) "The Story" was recorded "live to tape" with all the performers playing and singing at the same time, rather than following the usual practice of having musicians record their parts separately then combining them into a master recording.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Faber-1)
"The Story" was released as a single in 2007. It was iTunes' Download of the Week in March 2007.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Visakowitz-4) Carlile has performed the song live on _The Tonight Show with Jay Leno_, _[Late Night with Conan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late\_Night\_with\_Conan\_O'Brien "Late Night with Conan O'Brien")_ and _The Early Show_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Scanlon-5)

## Chart performance and reception
[edit]
In the United States Brandi Carlile's "The Story" reached No.75 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100 chart, as well as No.35 on the Adult Pop Songs chart and No.48 on the Digital Songs chart.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Visakowitz-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-allmusiccharts-6) The song peaked at No.44 on the Australian ARIA Singles Chart, No.3 on the Norwegian VG-lista chart, No.16 on the Swiss singles chart and No.38 on the Ö3 Austria Top 40 chart.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-AusCharts-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-NorChart-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-ChChart-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-AutChart-10)

## Chart performance and reception
Tom Scanlon of _The Seattle Times_ describes a live performance of "The Story" as "stunning" and "spine-chilling". He notes the transition within the song between acoustic pop-rock and "scream-singing" that resembles Janis Joplin.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Scanlon-5) A writer for _Indianapolis Monthly_ also draws a comparison between Carlile's vocals and those of Joplin.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-IM-11)_Billboard_ and _American Songwriter_ ranked the song number two and number four, respectively, on their lists of the 10 greatest Brandi Carlile songs.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-13)

This weekend while listening to Apple Music, I heard a lovely song by American singer-songwriter Brandi Carlile (b. 1981), “The Story.”
Today in Winnipeg, Canada, it’s a sunny spring-like day, after a winter that hardly was winter. Don’t get me wrong, we did get some chill-you-to-the-bone and wind-blowing-right-through-you days though not that many, and not for weeks or months on end. So it feels a bit weird and premature to be thinking of all things spring; and one thing in particular: a flooded back lane.
There’s a sewer drain a few houses away from ours and, since moving here in the early 00s, I somehow became the designated clearer of the catch basin. In autumn, it’s leaves and other stuff blocking rain from going into the sewer. In spring, the drain is frozen and surrounded by ice as the municipality doesn’t clear the snow often, and certainly not down to the concrete like they do on the roads.
So, as the snow melts, the melt water has nowhere to go but sideways and, as our 100-plus-year-old garage is not raised, it’s been flooded the odd time if I didn’t get out soon enough or simply couldn’t clear it because of the ice being too thick. From the time the melt starts, I usually have a couple of days before the water gets to a level where it’ll enter the garage. Yesterday, it was barely melting. Today, it is going like there’s no tomorrow, and the water was already lapping at the garage door. And it would take several days to get a City crew out.

So, out I went with my rubber boots (does anyone call them Wellingtons anymore?), Dad’s old heavy metal shovel, and my axe. It’s always a bit of a challenge to locate exactly where the drain is under a foot of water. But I can usually get my bearings by feeling the contours of the lane with my boots, to zero in on where to focus my efforts. Bashing away with the shovel and axe, soon there was music to my ears… that elusive sucking sound when water is rushing down a drain. Yay!!! I then chipped and shovelled down to the concrete for about 20 metres (60 feet) to create a channel from our property to the drain. (Past our place, no one else usually has an issue due to the slope of the lane.) It was a tiring but satisfying hour.
The back lane drain, released of ice and back in service.
Some neighbours have characterized my back lane drain-tending as devotion to the ‘hood. It’s pretty great when folks walk or drive by while I’m chipping away and wave or call out to thank me that they haven’t had to walk or drive through a foot of water. (And even better when drivers slow down so I don’t get splashed!). That’s my story.
Carlile’s story is also one of devotion.

In a 2013 interview with _\_Songfacts\__, contributor Dan MacIntosh asked her about people’s perceptions about songs and their meanings. She said, _“I used to speculate a lot about all my favorite songs and what they were about and what that means to me and what that must have manifested itself as. But there’s a lot between the lines. And fans have their own feelings and their own thoughts between the lines that you’ve actually written. And that’s what songs are for, is interpretation. They’re malleable. They can be made to be about one’s life. If it’s a love song, it can very easily be interpreted as a song about someone’s parents. If it’s about addiction, it could very easily be interpreted as being about a divorce or death. It’s relative. And that’s what I love about the art of songwriting.”_
“The Story,” which _Songfacts_ calls Carlile’s breakout hit song, is clearly about dedication to others and gratitude for companionship and support. And whether it’s a romantic attachment or the deepest of friendships, I don’t think it matters. The important thing is being connected and knowing someone will be there for you, like you were for them, like dealing with a flood, literally or figuratively.
I immediately recognized Carlile’s voice in the song, and just like the first time I heard her, I was swept away by the incredible things she does with her beautiful voice in this power ballad. Shivers… and not because I am wet and cold from bashing and splashing outside.
“The Story” is the title track from Carlile’s second studio album, released in 2007.
Now you know a little about why this is my _Song of the Day for Today_. I’m glad you stopped in.

And, don’t forget to check your drains.
Warmly,
_Steve_

"**The Story**" is a song released as a single by American folk rock singer Brandi Carlile, written by Phil Hanseroth, from her 2007 album _The Story_. It’s one of Carlile's best-known songs and has been included in the setlist of all of her concert tours to date.
The song was featured in _[Grey's Anatomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's\_Anatomy "Grey's Anatomy")_ on April 12, 2007 and is on [Grey's Anatomy Soundtrack album 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Anatomy_(soundtrack) "Grey's Anatomy (soundtrack)") (released September 11, 2007). It received renewed attention when a cover version was recorded by _Grey's Anatomy_ actor Sara Ramirez and included in the 2011 musical episode "Song Beneath the Song". The track was later covered by LeAnn Rimes for her _Remnants_ album, and by Dolly Parton for the charity tribute album _Cover Stories_.

## Composition and recording
[edit]
Twin brothers Phil and Tim Hanseroth have been Carlile's performing and writing partners since 2004[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Faber-1) and "The Story" was written by Phil Hanseroth before the Hanseroths began collaborating with Carlile.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Chinen-2) It has a 16-bar melody.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Chinen-2) It was recorded in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada and produced by T-Bone Burnett.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-3) "The Story" was recorded "live to tape" with all the performers playing and singing at the same time, rather than following the usual practice of having musicians record their parts separately then combining them into a master recording.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Faber-1)
"The Story" was released as a single in 2007. It was iTunes' Download of the Week in March 2007.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Visakowitz-4) Carlile has performed the song live on _The Tonight Show with Jay Leno_, _[Late Night with Conan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late\_Night\_with\_Conan\_O'Brien "Late Night with Conan O'Brien")_ and _The Early Show_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_(Brandi_Carlile_song)#cite_note-Scanlon-5)

This weekend while listening to Apple Music, I heard a lovely song by American singer-songwriter Brandi Carlile (b. 1981), “The Story.”
Today in Winnipeg, Canada, it’s a sunny spring-like day, after a winter that hardly was winter. Don’t get me wrong, we did get some chill-you-to-the-bone and wind-blowing-right-through-you days though not that many, and not for weeks or months on end. So it feels a bit weird and premature to be thinking of all things spring; and one thing in particular: a flooded back lane.
There’s a sewer drain a few houses away from ours and, since moving here in the early 00s, I somehow became the designated clearer of the catch basin. In autumn, it’s leaves and other stuff blocking rain from going into the sewer. In spring, the drain is frozen and surrounded by ice as the municipality doesn’t clear the snow often, and certainly not down to the concrete like they do on the roads.
So, as the snow melts, the melt water has nowhere to go but sideways and, as our 100-plus-year-old garage is not raised, it’s been flooded the odd time if I didn’t get out soon enough or simply couldn’t clear it because of the ice being too thick. From the time the melt starts, I usually have a couple of days before the water gets to a level where it’ll enter the garage. Yesterday, it was barely melting. Today, it is going like there’s no tomorrow, and the water was already lapping at the garage door. And it would take several days to get a City crew out.

So, out I went with my rubber boots (does anyone call them Wellingtons anymore?), Dad’s old heavy metal shovel, and my axe. It’s always a bit of a challenge to locate exactly where the drain is under a foot of water. But I can usually get my bearings by feeling the contours of the lane with my boots, to zero in on where to focus my efforts. Bashing away with the shovel and axe, soon there was music to my ears… that elusive sucking sound when water is rushing down a drain. Yay!!! I then chipped and shovelled down to the concrete for about 20 metres (60 feet) to create a channel from our property to the drain. (Past our place, no one else usually has an issue due to the slope of the lane.) It was a tiring but satisfying hour.
The back lane drain, released of ice and back in service.
Some neighbours have characterized my back lane drain-tending as devotion to the ‘hood. It’s pretty great when folks walk or drive by while I’m chipping away and wave or call out to thank me that they haven’t had to walk or drive through a foot of water. In a 2013 interview with _\_Songfacts\__, contributor Dan MacIntosh asked her about people’s perceptions about songs and their meanings. She said, _“I used to speculate a lot about all my favorite songs and what they were about and what that means to me and what that must have manifested itself as. But there’s a lot between the lines. And fans have their own feelings and their own thoughts between the lines that you’ve actually written. And that’s what songs are for, is interpretation. They’re malleable. They can be made to be about one’s life. If it’s a love song, it can very easily be interpreted as a song about someone’s parents. If it’s about addiction, it could very easily be interpreted as being about a divorce or death. It’s relative. And that’s what I love about the art of songwriting.”_
“The Story,” which _Songfacts_ calls Carlile’s breakout hit song, is clearly about dedication to others and gratitude for companionship and support. And whether it’s a romantic attachment or the deepest of friendships, I don’t think it matters. The important thing is being connected and knowing someone will be there for you, like you were for them, like dealing with a flood, literally or figuratively.
I immediately recognized Carlile’s voice in the song, and just like the first time I heard her, I was swept away by the incredible things she does with her beautiful voice in this power ballad. Shivers… and not because I am wet and cold from bashing and splashing outside.
“The Story” is the title track from Carlile’s second studio album, released in 2007.

Her bandmate Phil Hanseroth wrote “The Story” before they even started playing together.
Since her debut, all of the music appearing under the name Brandi Carlile has been the product of an extraordinarily close partnership of Carlile and the twin brothers Tim and Phil Hanseroth. All three write songs and share the writing credits equally for every song regardless of who contributes what (à la Lennon and McCartney).
The three musicians connected in Seattle, where the twins played in the hard-rock band the Fighting Machinists while Carlile, raised on Patsy Cline and the Grand Ole Opry, was busking and doing bar gigs.
After the Fighting Machinists disbanded, Carlile recruited the twins to play with her; they first performed together in 2000, got matching tattoos (of the auryn talisman from _The NeverEnding Story,_ a movie they all loved as kids), and started collaborating on songs rooted in country, rock, and folk.
In this excerpt from a 2014 interview with me for _Acoustic Guitar_ magazine _,_ Carlile and the twins spoke with me about “The Story” and their style of collaboration.
The full interview is available is the May 2015 issue of _Acoustic Guitar_ or on Patreon.

### The story behind "The Story"
_It’s so hard to imagine that “The Story” existed before you started playing together. How did the original version compare with Brandi’s version?_
PHIL It doesn’t even compare at all. We had recorded a couple versions, like one on a keyboard and one with acoustic guitars. It was just a lyric, a melody, a couple of chords—it wasn’t really anything until we started playing with Brandi and she was able to put some power into it.
BRANDI “The Story” was already a beautiful song. Phil’s got a really powerful voice and sounded great singing it. But I think the song needed to be really loved by someone. If anything, I brought to the scenario a little bit of insanity and intensity and cultishness. Especially when I was younger, I was a little overwhelming. I came on the scene and I was like, “All right, let’s quit our jobs and get matching tattoos and never look back! I don’t care—forget about your wives, forget about everything, let’s just do this!”
TIM When we first met Brandi, she was playing primarily acoustic guitar, and my brother and I were still playing only electric guitar in a hard rock band. It was such an odd thing. We met Brandi and got into the acoustic guitar with her, and then six months later we were both getting divorces and had a bunch of tattoos, I swear! It was a big shift for everyone musically, and also we found our Charles Manson [_laughter_]. My brother and I have always had a close musical thing, but we finally found our third sibling.
_How would you characterize each other’s strengths as songwriters?_
BRANDI Well, I’ve got a pretty good grip on that. Phil writes these interesting and androgynous powerhouse songs, very infrequently. They’re usually kind of strange lyrically. I don’t think he really forces it. “Blood Muscle Skin & Bone,” “The Story,” “Oh Dear,” “Beginning to Feel the Years”—those are some of our more quirky _Pet Sounds_ type tunes, and they come from the terrifying mind of Phil.
texts.2:
### The story behind "The Story"
And then Tim, in my opinion, is your classic, workman-style songwriter who writes so many more songs than Phil and I do, and he writes them with such strength and continuity. I think they are our flagship songs on every record. When you hear a song that was started or penned by Tim, it sounds like the Brandi Carlile trio.
With me, it’s a real crap shoot, because it has to do so much with what’s going on in my life, and it’s based solely on lyrics. I tend to focus on my feelings and my environment lyrically. I like to really say what I mean and mean what I say, and say things that are special. So all three of us bring something interesting to the band. Tim brings total consistency and a prolific nature, Phil brings eccentricity, and I bring communication.
_Why did you decide to share songwriting credits for all of your songs?_
BRANDI Because there’s no ego. The music wins and takes precedence. Nobody questions anybody else if they really think that a bridge would make a song better or a lyric should change or we could add more interesting chords.
TIM It’s been like that since the very beginning. When we first met, it was like, hey, if we’re going to write songs together, let’s just split everything up. That way you’re not stuck being in a band with someone who’s doing really really well—
BRANDI Driving a red car.
TIM We all end up having to tour the same amount together, we spend an incredible amount of time together, and even though one of us may write a song that’s a hit for ten years, like Phil did here, we’re all putting about the same amount of work into it.
We don’t get too precious about our songwriting. If one of us has an idea that’s half done, nobody’s going to get possessive because they want the credit for it. Nobody’s going to get their feelings hurt by going, yeah, I want to write this one alone. We are all really open to just the song being the best.
_On the albums, though, you do credit who individually wrote each song. Why?_
texts.3:
### The story behind "The Story"
BRANDI For me, just because my heroes do. When I read the liner notes, I want to know. I’m really big into entertainers, and when I love an artist, I love everything about them. I love their philanthropy, I love their biography, their childhood stories, their artwork, the liner notes, and the songwriting. If I hear a song that I think is deeply personal, I want to know who wrote it and if it’s about what I think it’s about.

The song became one of Carlile's signature songs and was featured prominently on her 2007 album of the same name. It gained additional popularity after being covered by actress Sara Ramirez on *Grey's Anatomy* in 2007, and later by LeAnn Rimes and Dolly Parton.

Interestingly, while Phil Hanseroth wrote the song, he has consistently shared songwriting credits with all members of their group, as is their collaborative tradition.
